There are a lot of instances of the blind leading the blind in fast food establishments.

In most places in the US, overtime won't kick in for hourly fast food employees unless they go over 40 hours for the week. The length of the shift generally won't matter.

Have you ever worked at a place where it wasn't a terminable offense to clock someone else in or out? I haven't.

Have you ever managed a fast-paced service environment before, or more specifically, teenagers or young adults? Managers having to edit the time records because someone messed up the simple process of clocking in or out is literally a daily occurrence. People forget to clock back in from breaks, when they arrive, or forget to clock out at the end of a shift.

For the specific situation mentioned, it may be malice, or it may be a lack of understanding of how the time clock system works (for the individual and other employees). One innocent explanation is that he may simply not be clocking off at the end of his shift every night. If the daytime manager is showing up every morning to find the closers still on the clock, standard procedure is going to be to clock them off for the time they were scheduled to leave the previous night. That's probably midnight.

They're not going to waste time trying to call the previous night's closers at 4:30 in the morning and will have forgotten about it by lunchtime. If no one complains about missing hours, they'll never spare a second thought about it because little things like this are literally a daily occurrence for that sort of job.

In fact, the whole closing crew might be forgetting to clock off every night because at some point in the past they just decided that you didn't have to because of the pile of clock out receipts generated at midnight, and the morning managers might be slowly going nuts because they think the night shift is full of people who can't work a time clock. There's often very little communication between shifts in these sorts of establishments, and issues like this can fester for months if the general manager isn't on top of things.

Are you on a low population server or a high population one? The strategy I would use is different depending on the population.

Either way, I'd put pressure on crafting materials. Buy them up until they are 15-20% over market value, and then flip or craft with them, depending on what makes more sense.

At that point, if on a high population server, I'd just keep the pressure on the materials and wait for the competitor to sell out or for their margins to erode to unprofitability. If on a low population server, I'd also undercut significantly so that they are faced with the choice of posting for a loss (at which point I'd buy them out and repost) or they back down.

If you are having an issue with this, I guess you're on a low population server. On a busy server, I deal with a lot of people camping and undercutting, but the issue is negligible because the volume of items sold turns over so fast that unless they post a large quantity, my items are still selling. People also tend to only post a single stack size, so if they are undercutting aggressively with singles, I just post above their prices in stacks, and vice versa.

On a low population server, you can pressure them until they aren't making a profit, but ultimately this will come down to the two of you comparing resources. The one willing to take the bigger loss during your game of auction house chicken wins. A better strategy might just be finding out when they typically post and putting yours up when they aren't camping.

One issue is that druid healing is currently balanced for a specific expansion, which has a very different style for healing compared to previous ones. Health pools are enormous, damage intake tends to be rather steady, and one-shot mechanics are pretty rare, so the heal-over-time spells are tuned for that environment. The overall design (outside of high-level dungeons and progression raiding) is for mistakes to impact the healers' mana rather than to kill players. Lower level content is the opposite, as the amount of damage dealt (compared to health pools) is much higher and the heal-over-time spells tick for comparatively lower values compared to the damage taken.

For lower level content, you will be using many more direct heals than you will at max level. Keep your direct healing spells ready to go and you should be fine. Also, don't hesitate to communicate with the tank that they need to make smaller pulls if you are struggling. Most people will understand. The type of tank you have will also affect your experience. Certain tank classes hardly need a healer due to the strength of their self-heals at low levels, while others are solid in terms of their damage mitigation. However, low-level tanks of a specific class can be challenging to heal if the player doesn't understand the class mechanics (which is unfortunate, because a well-played tank of that class synergizes really well with a druid healer).

Content from a specific expansion will be the most challenging portion of leveling as a healer, as the one-shot mechanics are prevalent, the damage output is punishing when players make mistakes, and the debuffs applied by enemies are tuned for an era when dispels weren't on a cooldown.
